description: Ostracism revived in a modern democracy: historical parameters of the Athenian institution, the state of modern research, a Fermi estimation of why the deterrence hypothesis (banishment risk reduces the supply of prominence-seekers) is a research gap, and a Fermi estimation of the gross and net behavioral effects of a modern ostracism with a communication ban.

words.name: ostracism (institution)
words.description: The Athenian political procedure (ostrakophoria): annual popular vote that could expel one citizen for ten years without accusation, trial or loss of property. Distinct from 'ostracism (social psychology)'.

words.name: ostracism (social psychology)
words.description: Interpersonal or workplace exclusion as studied in social psychology (Williams tradition). Dominates the modern research literature under the keyword 'ostracism'; a different construct from the political institution.

words.name: neo-ostracism
words.description: Malkopoulou's proposal: a revived, modernized ostracism as a participatory mechanism of democratic self-defence (temporary exclusion by public vote instead of judicial party bans).

words.name: communication-ban variant
words.description: Design variant from this dialogue: instead of physical exile, the ostracized person is barred from public communication and office for the exclusion period, so that internet reach does not neutralize the measure.

words.name: quorum 6000 (participation reading)
words.description: Reading A of the Athenian 6000 threshold: at least 6000 ballots had to be cast in total for the ostracism to be valid.

words.name: quorum 6000 (against-one-person reading)
words.description: Reading B of the Athenian 6000 threshold: at least 6000 votes had to name the same person. The sources (Plutarch vs. Philochoros) support different readings; both are kept as separate words instead of a free-text note.

words.name: prominence seeker
words.description: A person actively investing in national-level public visibility (politics, media, platforms). Unit of the deterrence Fermi estimation.

words.name: top-tier exposure group
words.description: The subset of prominence seekers with realistic annual risk of being named in an ostracism vote (most visible / most polarizing).

words.name: idle candidate
words.description: In the Galasso/Nannicini/Nunnari experiments: the candidate who neither attacks nor is attacked; beneficiary of the attention-redistribution (spillover) effect.

words.name: attention substitution
words.description: Mechanism: visibility vacated by a removed or deterred figure is largely captured by replacement figures instead of disappearing. Limits the net effect of ostracism on total prominence-seeking.

words.name: Switzerland
words.description: Reference polity for the effect estimation (population about 9 million, direct-democratic instruments, cantonal recall rights).

values.name: athens last ostracism year
values.description: Hyperbolos; dating disputed between 417 and 415 BC.

values.name: athens exclusion duration
values.description: Property and citizenship retained; no formal accusation required.

values.name: athens vote threshold
values.description: See words 'quorum 6000 (participation reading)' and 'quorum 6000 (against-one-person reading)' for the two source traditions.

values.name: athens attested ostracized individuals
values.description: Securely to plausibly attested ostracisms over the roughly 70-year practice period; scholarly counts vary.

values.name: modern implementations of political ostracism
values.description: No contemporary democracy operates an ostracism-type institution (temporary exclusion of one named person by general popular vote without accusation). Recall elections and impeachment are related but distinct (they target office-holders for cause or performance).

values.name: idle-candidate vote share gain, field experiment
values.description: Increase in the idle candidate's vote share when the incumbent was attacked by the other challenger; Italian mayoral race, randomized canvassing.

values.name: idle-candidate relative gain, field experiment
values.description: The 3.7 pp gain relative to the idle candidate's average vote share.

values.name: idle-candidate share, survey experiment, positive campaign
idle-candidate share, survey experiment, negative neutral campaign
idle-candidate share, survey experiment, negative aggressive campaign
empirical studies per implemented removal institution
values.description: Order-of-magnitude rate at which an actually implemented negative-selection institution (e.g. US recall elections) accumulates empirical studies. Anchored on the recall literature size.

values.name: prominence seekers, national level, Switzerland
values.description: National and cantonal politicians plus media figures and platform creators actively investing in national visibility.

values.name: top-tier exposure group size
values.description: Persons with realistic annual risk of being named; the risk is heavily concentrated at the top of the visibility distribution.

values.name: ostracisms per year
values.description: Design parameter from the dialogue: exactly one person per year, as in Athens.

values.name: exposed career length
values.description: Years a top-tier figure typically stays in the exposure group.

values.name: risk aversion multiplier
values.description: Behavioral weight: a 10-year communication ban is a catastrophic, non-insurable career loss, so decision weight exceeds the raw probability (loss aversion).

values.name: attention substitution fraction
values.description: Share of vacated attention captured by replacement figures. Anchored qualitatively on the strong idle-candidate spillover in src_galasso2021 and on the attention-concentration findings in the attention_scarcity dataset: audience demand for focal figures persists even when a specific figure is removed.

formulas.name: expected empirical ostracism studies
formulas.expression: modern implementations of political ostracism * empirical studies per implemented removal institution
formulas.description: 0 implementations x 20 studies per institution = 0 expected empirical studies. Core of the research-gap explanation: the empirical literature tracks implemented institutions, and ostracism has none.

formulas.name: annual naming risk, top tier
formulas.expression: ostracisms per year / top-tier exposure group size

formulas.name: career naming risk, top tier
formulas.expression: annual naming risk, top tier * exposed career length
formulas.description: Linear approximation of cumulative risk over the exposed career; acceptable for small annual probabilities.

formulas.name: gross deterrence fraction, top tier
formulas.expression: career naming risk, top tier * risk aversion multiplier
formulas.description: Fraction of top-tier aspirants expected to abandon or substantially moderate prominence-seeking when a credible ostracism with communication ban exists. Supports the dialogue hypothesis at the top tier.

formulas.name: net reduction in prominence-seeking supply
formulas.expression: gross deterrence fraction, top tier * attention retained after substitution
formulas.description: Net system-level effect after replacement figures fill vacated attention. The gross effect on individuals is large; the net effect on total prominence is roughly 5 to 10 times smaller because of attention substitution.

claims.name: research gap exists
claims.statement: No empirical study tests whether a banishment-type risk reduces the number of people seeking political or media prominence.
claims.basis: Targeted searches 2026-10-10 found political theory on ostracism revival (src_malkopoulou2017, src_salamanca2023, src_cordis, src_johnson2010) and adjacent empirics (negative campaigning, public-goods experiments), but no study of the deterrence-of-prominence hypothesis.

claims.name: gap reason 1: no implementation, no data
claims.statement: Empirical political science follows implemented institutions; with 0 modern implementations there is no observational or quasi-experimental data on political ostracism.

claims.name: gap reason 2: keyword occupied
claims.statement: The keyword 'ostracism' is dominated by social-psychology research on interpersonal exclusion, which lowers the visibility of the institutional question in literature searches and citation networks.

claims.name: gap reason 3: disciplinary split
claims.statement: The hypothesis requires linking normative institutional design (political theory) with the psychology and economics of fame-seeking (behavioral science); these communities rarely co-author.

claims.name: dialogue hypothesis: strong deterrence
claims.statement: A credible ostracism with a temporary communication ban would strongly reduce the number of people who want to become prominent (Timon's hypothesis).
claims.basis: Supported at the individual top-tier level by the gross deterrence estimate (0.4); weakened at the system level by attention substitution (net 0.08).

claims.name: dialogue hypothesis: redistribution is the goal
claims.statement: Strategic coordination of ostracism votes redistributes attention more evenly, which is the intended effect rather than a failure mode (Timon's reframing of the Hyperbolos objection).
claims.basis: Consistent with the idle-candidate spillover evidence in src_galasso2021: removing or damaging focal figures measurably shifts support to less polarizing third parties.

claims.name: dialogue hypothesis: silence prevents martyrdom
claims.statement: A ten-year communication ban prevents the martyr effect because the narrative cannot be sustained without the person's own presence (Timon).
claims.basis: Plausible; residual risk is narrative carriage by successors.

claims.name: counterpoint: enforcement cost
claims.statement: Enforcing a genuine communication ban in the internet era requires surveillance of the person and their network (ghostwriters, proxies, quotation by third parties); this enforcement infrastructure is itself a power concentration (Claude).

claims.name: counterpoint: selection shift
claims.statement: A career-ending tail risk shifts the composition of prominence seekers toward the risk-tolerant and those with little to lose, not necessarily toward the moderate (Claude).

claims.name: legal constraint
claims.statement: Physical exile of own nationals conflicts with ICCPR Art. 12(4); a communication ban additionally engages freedom of expression (Swiss Const. Art. 16, ECHR Art. 10, ICCPR Art. 19). The ICCPR provides no denunciation clause per the Human Rights Committee, so a constitutional carve-out would mean an open treaty breach.

open_questions: Empirical test design: recall-election jurisdictions as natural experiment - does candidate entry or incumbent rhetoric differ where recall exists? Nearest feasible proxy for the deterrence hypothesis.
Does the gross deterrence effect (0.4) select against the cautious and in favor of the reckless (counterpoint: selection shift)?
Measured value needed: actual size of the recall-election empirical literature, to replace the assumed 20 studies per institution.
Authors of src_jebo_ostracism to be verified before any reuse.
